title: NURS 1017 Unit 3 Case Study 5

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which of the following findings would be consistent with Turner syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Temperature 36.7° C and SpO₂ 99% on room air
Webbed neck, low posterior hairline, and broad chest with widely spaced nipples
Height of 142 cm, below the 3rd percentile for age
No breast development (Tanner stage 1) and no menstrual periods at age 15
Tanner stage 2 pubic hair
Difficulty with visual-spatial math despite strong overall grades
No history of headaches or changes in vision
Right arm BP 138/84 mm Hg, right thigh BP 98/60 mm Hg, and weak, delayed femoral pulses

question.explanation:
Consistent with Turner syndrome (45,X): short stature is the most constant feature (Option 3). Streak ovaries make too little estrogen, so breasts do not develop and menstruation does not begin (Option 4). Lymphatic swelling before birth leaves a webbed neck and low hairline, with a broad, shield-like chest (Option 2).

Higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs, with weak, delayed femoral pulses, points to coarctation of the aorta, a heart defect common in Turner syndrome (Option 8). Normally, thigh BP is equal to or higher than arm BP.

Intelligence is usually normal, but many girls with Turner syndrome have a specific difficulty with visual-spatial tasks such as geometry (Option 6).

Not consistent: pubic hair comes from adrenal androgens (adrenarche), which Turner syndrome does not affect, so Tanner stage 2 pubic hair does not point to it (Option 5). No headaches or vision changes makes a pituitary tumor less likely as a cause of delayed puberty, but says nothing for or against Turner syndrome (Option 7). Temperature and SpO₂ are normal (Option 1).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a pediatric endocrinology clinic is assessing Chloe, a 15-year-old female client referred by her primary care provider for short stature and no menstrual periods.

question.stem: The nurse prepares teaching that compares sex chromosome disorders. For each characteristic, click to specify whether it applies to Turner syndrome (45,X), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), or both.

rows.text: 45 chromosomes; short stature and webbed neck
Primary gonadal failure with high FSH and LH, and infertility in most affected individuals
47 chromosomes; tall stature, small firm testes, and gynecomastia
Coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, and horseshoe kidney
Usually arises by chance from an error in chromosome separation, not from an inherited single-gene mutation
Low testosterone, sparse facial and body hair, and language-based learning difficulties

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1030 (Week 2) and the Diagnostic Results.
question.explanation:
Turner syndrome (45,X): one X chromosome is missing (monosomy X), so cells have 45 chromosomes. Loss of genes on the second X causes short stature, a webbed neck, a shield chest, streak ovaries, a horseshoe kidney, and heart defects (coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve).

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): a male with an extra X chromosome (47 chromosomes). The testes become small and firm and make little testosterone, causing tall stature with long legs, gynecomastia, sparse body hair, infertility, and language-based learning difficulties.

Both: each is a sex chromosome aneuploidy that usually arises by chance, from nondisjunction during gamete formation (or, in Turner syndrome, loss of an X chromosome in early cell divisions, which explains mosaic forms). Down syndrome (47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21) arises the same way, but involves an autosome (chromosome 21), not a sex chromosome. Both conditions cause primary gonadal failure: the gonads do not respond, so the pituitary releases more FSH and LH, and most affected people are infertile. The parents did not pass on a faulty gene.

leftContent.intro: Two weeks later, Chloe and her mother return to review the karyotype, hormone levels, pelvic ultrasound and echocardiogram.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Chloe's karyotype shows [[drop0]], which usually arises by chance. The nurse's priority is [[drop1]]. Her absent breast development and menstrual periods are caused by [[drop2]].

options.text: trisomy of chromosome 21
a single-gene mutation inherited from a carrier parent
an extra X chromosome (47,XXY)
monosomy X (45 chromosomes)
disturbed body image related to her short stature
high blood pressure in the arms from coarctation of the aorta
the limited time left for growth before the growth plates close
the risk of kidney injury from the horseshoe kidney
an absent uterus from abnormal development
a pituitary gland that releases too little FSH and LH
streak ovaries that make little estrogen, so FSH and LH rise
low body weight suppressing the hypothalamus

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1115 (Week 2).
question.explanation:
Monosomy X: normal cells have 46 chromosomes (22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes). In Turner syndrome one X is missing, leaving 45. An extra X (47,XXY) is Klinefelter syndrome, and trisomy 21 is Down syndrome.

Priority: coarctation makes the left ventricle pump against a narrowed aorta. Her arm BP is rising (140/86 mm Hg) and her legs tire with exertion. Untreated, it leads to left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and, with a bicuspid valve, aortic dilation and dissection. The horseshoe kidney (normal creatinine), her growth window and her body image all matter, but they are not a threat to her circulation now.

Cause of absent puberty: high FSH and LH with low estradiol mean the problem lies in the ovaries (primary or hypergonadotropic hypogonadism): the pituitary is signalling hard and the streak ovaries cannot respond. A pituitary problem would give low FSH and LH. The ultrasound shows a uterus, and her weight (15th percentile) and lack of strenuous training do not suggest hypothalamic suppression.

leftContent.intro: The nurse reviews Chloe's results with the endocrinologist and cardiologist to set care priorities.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in Chloe's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange cardiology follow-up and teach the family that the aorta and heart valve need lifelong monitoring
Schedule screening for hypothyroidism, hearing loss, and celiac disease
Teach Chloe how to give testosterone injections to speed up her growth
Explain that low-dose estrogen, increased slowly, will promote breast development and protect bone density
Acknowledge Chloe's feelings about fertility and offer a Turner syndrome peer support group
Tell Chloe that once estrogen therapy starts, her ovaries will begin releasing eggs
Teach Chloe and her mother how to give the daily subcutaneous growth hormone injection

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1300 (Week 2) and the Care Plan.
question.explanation:
Include: coarctation and a bicuspid aortic valve need lifelong cardiology follow-up, even after repair (Option 1). Growth hormone works only while the growth plates are open, so daily injections start now; the nurse teaches the technique and site rotation (Option 7). Estrogen started at a low dose and increased slowly brings on breast development and protects bone without closing the growth plates too early (Option 4). Chloe is grieving the likely loss of fertility; acknowledging it and offering peer support helps her cope, and egg donation can be discussed later (Option 5). Turner syndrome raises the lifetime risk of autoimmune thyroid disease, hearing loss and celiac disease (Option 2).

Do not include: estrogen replaces the hormone the ovaries cannot make, but it does not create egg follicles, so it does not restore fertility (Option 6). Testosterone treats the hormone deficit of males with Klinefelter syndrome; it has no place in Turner syndrome (Option 3).

leftContent.intro: The nurse works with cardiology, endocrinology and psychosocial services on Chloe's plan of care.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Measure BP in all four limbs and compare the radial and femoral pulses
Tell Chloe that estrogen alone, without a progestin, can be taken long term
Explain that estrogen starts at a low dose and is increased slowly to protect her final height
Request a sweat chloride test to look for another cause of her short stature
Explain that Turner syndrome usually occurs by chance and is not caused by a gene her sister could carry
Tell Chloe that cardiology follow-up can stop once the coarctation is repaired

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 0930 (Week 6) and the Vital Signs.
question.explanation:
Measure BP in all four limbs (Indicated): the arm-to-leg gradient (40 mm Hg today) and femoral pulses show how severe the coarctation is and give a baseline for judging the repair.

Estrogen alone long term (Contraindicated): in anyone with a uterus, estrogen without a progestin causes endometrial hyperplasia and raises the risk of endometrial cancer. A cyclic progestin is added after breakthrough bleeding or about 2 years of estrogen.

Low dose, increased slowly (Indicated): full adult doses early would close the growth plates quickly and cut short the height gained with growth hormone; a slow increase also gives more natural breast development.

Sweat chloride test (Non-Essential): it diagnoses cystic fibrosis. Her short stature is explained by the 45,X karyotype; the test adds nothing.

Explain the sporadic cause (Indicated): 45,X Turner syndrome is a chance error in chromosome separation, not a Mendelian gene, so her sister's risk is not increased and she does not need testing because of Chloe's diagnosis.

Stop cardiology follow-up after repair (Contraindicated): after repair, people with Turner syndrome and a bicuspid valve remain at risk of re-narrowing, high blood pressure, and aortic dilation and dissection, so follow-up is lifelong.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Chloe's growth velocity of 7.5 cm/year, equal arm and leg blood pressures, and Tanner stage 2 breast development show [[drop0]]. When Chloe explains that her 45,X chromosome makeup is her [[drop1]] and her short stature is her phenotype, she shows understanding. Before she moves to adult care, the nurse confirms she understands that she needs [[drop2]].

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1000 (Month 12), the Vital Signs, and the Follow-Up Results.
question.explanation:
Response to treatment: growth velocity rose from 2.1 to 7.5 cm/year on growth hormone, the arm-to-leg BP gradient is gone (thigh BP now above arm BP, as expected), and estrogen has started breast development. Without treatment, girls with Turner syndrome do not have a pubertal growth spurt. She is still growing, so growth hormone continues until growth slows and the growth plates close. Treatment does not change the karyotype.

Genotype and phenotype: the genotype is the genetic (here chromosomal) makeup, 45,X. The phenotype is what can be observed: short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries.

Lifelong follow-up: even after a good repair, she remains at risk of re-narrowing, hypertension and aortic dilation or dissection (higher in pregnancy), and needs ongoing estrogen and progestin, thyroid, hearing and bone monitoring as an adult.

tabs.title: Care Plan
tabs.content:
TeamPlan
Pediatric cardiologyTranscatheter treatment of the coarctation (balloon angioplasty or stent). Echocardiogram or cardiac MRI at regular intervals for the bicuspid valve and aortic root.
Pediatric endocrinologyRecombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) subcutaneously every evening. Low-dose transdermal estradiol, increased slowly; cyclic progestin added after breakthrough bleeding or about 2 years of estrogen.
Primary careYearly TSH and free T4; hearing tests; celiac disease screening; bone mineral density scan.
Psychosocial and geneticsCounselling for body image and loss of fertility; genetic counselling about the sporadic cause and future options for having children.
